entries.title: Aicruae Funeral Traditions
entries.text:
Aicruae Funeral Traditions
Aicruae — Funeral Customs
A culture's grief made visible. The Aicruan funeral is not private. It marks the
mourner's body, the road they walk, and the air around them. The dead do not
simply leave — they are sent.
Quick Facts
Cultural Philosophy Grief is public, ritualized, and physically inscribed on the
mourner's body
Deities Invoked
(multiple — see below)
Razar (the soul's ascent), Nellebrie (the disaster of loss), and
others depending on relationship and region
No Single Death Deity
Aicruae has no specific god of death or the underworld.
Funerals are polytheistic — different gods are invoked for
different aspects of the loss.
Disposition of the Body Class-coded. Royalty and high nobility are entombed.
Commoners are cremated on pyres.
Universal Ritual Items Iksyre (headdress), Broep (chain veil), red paint markings, bare
feet, the Geina, a strand of the deceased's hair
Gendered Element Male mourners wear an Eye Bind (sheer black cloth). Female
mourners do not.
The Polytheistic Funeral
Aicruae has no single god of death or the underworld. This shapes funeral
practice profoundly. Where a culture with a death god might funnel all funeral
prayers through one deity, Aicruan funerals invoke multiple gods — each for a
specific aspect of what is happening.
Razar Sun God) — for the soul's ascent.
The smoke from the burning hair and the Geina rises toward the sun. Razar
Aicruae Funeral T raditions
1
receives it. The body, whether buried or burned, is mortal flesh that returns to its
element; the soul ascends as smoke. Every Aicruan funeral, regardless of class or
region, invokes Razar.
Nellebrie Goddess of Disasters) — for the disaster of the loss itself.
A death is not just a death. It is a disaster for those left behind. Nellebrie is invoked
not as a death deity but as the goddess who presides over what is now broken —
the household without its head, the regiment without its captain, the child without
their parent. She is invoked to acknowledge that something has been destroyed
by this loss, not just changed. This is why Solis chose to bury Princess Iris and
Prince Orcus beneath a temple of Nellebrie at Rewqo. The Aicruan Civil War was
the disaster. Burying its victims at her temple was a confession dressed as
devotion. INFERRED — confirm reading.]
Other deities invoked depending on context.
Paha Goddess of Horses, Nellebrie's mother) — for those who died in cavalry
service or whose families work with horses
Zopha Sea Goddess) — for fishermen, sailors, and those who died at sea
(heavily invoked in Northern Aicruae)
TBD additional deities] — confirm which other gods in the Aicruan pantheon
get specific funeral invocations and under what circumstances
Class and Regional Variation
Noble funerals tend to invoke more deities than commoner funerals — partly
because nobles can afford longer ceremonies, partly because invoking more gods
is a status display. Regional variation is significant: a Northern Isles fisherman's
funeral might invoke Razar and Zopha primarily, with Nellebrie only briefly. A noble
funeral in Lajazer might invoke five or six deities across an extended ceremony.
The Mourner's Regalia
The Iksyre — Ceremonial Headdress
A flat, circular headdress worn atop the head by mourners during funerary rites.
The Iksyre is a symbol of grief, humility, and reverence for the dead.
Aicruae Funeral T raditions
2
The Noble Iksyre
The full ceremonial Iksyre is a heavy, flat steel disk — circular, often etched with
sacred markings or family sigils on its upper face. Beneath it hangs the Broep. It is
worn by nobles and royal mourners during formal funerary processions.
The Commoner's Iksyre
Commoners construct their own makeshift Iksyres. The shape and meaning are
the same — a flat circular disk worn atop the head — but the materials are
whatever a household can afford or improvise. INFERRED: likely wood, leather,
woven reed, or hammered tin in place of steel; the chains beneath may be twine,
rope, or simple cord rather than steel and wire. Confirm specifics or leave open
for regional variation.]
Symbolism
The flat circle echoes Razar's disk in the sky. To wear it is to bow under the sun's
witness. The mourner does not stand in their own light during grief — they stand
under his.
The Broep — Chain Veil
A veil of interlinked steel chains and wire that hangs from the lower edge of the
Iksyre. It obscures the mourner's face from the world, severing them from the
living for the duration of the rite.
The Broep is heavy. Wearing it is uncomfortable. This is intentional — grief is a
weight, and the Broep makes the weight visible.
The chains end in small weighted beads or drops, which sway and click softly as
the mourner moves. The sound carries during processions and is sometimes
called the rain of the dead in older Aicruan poetry. INFERRED — may not be
canon; flag for confirmation.]
For commoners, the makeshift Broep may be made of simpler materials — strips
of dark cloth, knotted twine, beaded cord, or thin chain salvaged from common
workshop scraps.
The Eye Bind — Male Mourners Only
A strip of translucent black cloth used to bind the eyes of male mourners. It
represents the turning inward and the refusal to witness the world in mourning.
Aicruae Funeral T raditions
3
Why male mourners only: INFERRED — needs your confirmation.] In Aicruae's
patriarchal culture, men hold the public weight of authority — they witness
contracts, validate truth in court, and "see" the kingdom into its decisions. The
Eye Bind inverts that authority during grief. By binding their eyes, they refuse to
witness the world while it has been diminished by loss. They will not legitimize the
death by looking on the world that allowed it. Female mourners do not need the
binding — their grief is expected to be visible through the markings and the
procession itself, not through refusal to see.
The cloth is sheer enough that the mourner can perceive shapes and movement,
but not faces or detail. Male mourners are typically guided by a younger relative or
a priestly attendant during the procession.
Body Preparation of the Mourner
The mourner's own body is marked and prepared as part of the rite.
Red Paint Markings
The mourner is painted with traditional red markings across the body — face,
neck, chest, arms, sometimes the back. These markings are paint, not tattoos.
They are washed away after the mourning period ends.
The patterns are traditional and likely vary by region and house. TBD — confirm:
are there standard mourning patterns? Sigils tied to specific houses? Marks
specific to relationship with the deceased (parent, spouse, child)?
The color is symbolic. Red is the color of life — blood, the heart, the warmth that
the body loses in death. To paint the mourner in red is to mark them as still living,
still bleeding warmth, while they walk beside someone who no longer can.
The Forehead Mark
A small red dot is placed at the center of the mourner's forehead, between the
brows. INFERRED meaning: the eye that does not close, the witness the soul
carries. Confirm or revise.]
Red Hands and Feet
Aicruae Funeral T raditions
4
The mourner's hands and feet are dyed deep red — not painted in patterns, but
fully colored. The dye soaks the skin and stains for days after the funeral.
Barefoot Procession
Mourners walk barefoot during funeral processions. Combined with the dyed feet,
this means they leave a trail of red footprints behind them as they walk.
This is the most striking visual element of an Aicruan funeral. The dead's path
through the living world is literally marked on the road. After the procession, the
footprints fade with rain and traffic, mirroring the way grief fades from public
memory while remaining inside the mourner's body.
TBD — does the funeral procession follow a specific route? From the home to the
temple? From the temple to the burial site or pyre? The route choice determines
where the red footprints accumulate, and may have political weight (e.g., a noble
funeral procession passing through commoner districts).]
The Geina and the Hair
Two items burn at every Aicruan funeral, regardless of class.
A Strand of the Dead's Hair
Cut from the deceased before the body is prepared. Burning the hair sends a part
of the deceased's physical self up to Razar with the smoke. It is the body's first
act of ascending, even before disposition.
The Geina — "Item Treasured"
Geina translates to item treasured. It is something the deceased loved — an object
they were known to cherish in life. It is given to the fire so that the deceased has
something familiar with them in their journey beyond.
The Geina is chosen by family or close friends, ideally someone who knew the
deceased intimately. The wrong Geina is considered a failure of love — a sign that
no one truly knew what the dead held dear.
Examples of Geinas in canon or implied by canon: TBD — open for additions.]
Aicruae Funeral T raditions
5
For mourners attending the funeral, watching the Geina burn is the moment they
say goodbye. The hair represents the body letting go. The Geina represents the
world letting go.
Disposition of the Body — Class-Coded
This is where Aicruae splits.
Royalty and High Nobility — Entombment
Royals and high-ranking nobles are buried, not burned. Their bodies are placed in
tombs, crypts, or beneath sacred sites. The body is preserved as monument; the
soul has already been sent upward through the Geina-and-hair burning.
Canonical examples:
Princess Iris Aleka Patton (died 7,218 BR, Battle of Rewqo) — buried by Solis
beneath a temple of Nellebrie at Rewqo
Prince Orcus Emere Patton (died after Iris) — buried by Solis at the same site,
beneath the same temple
Implications: Noble tombs are political objects. Where a noble is buried, what's
etched on the tomb, who is allowed to visit — these are statements of power. Solis
burying Iris and Orcus together beneath a temple of Nellebrie is doing several
things at once: marking them as honored dead, claiming them permanently,
framing the civil war that killed them as a disaster under Nellebrie's domain, and
binding them to a sacred site he chose. This is consistent with the cultural rule
and also reads as a possessive act on his part. The choice of Nellebrie's temple
specifically — Goddess of Disasters — is its own confession. Solis was naming
what he had done.
Tomb construction: TBD — who builds noble tombs? Are they prepared in
advance during the noble's lifetime, or commissioned after death? Family crypts
vs. temple-affiliated burials? Grave goods?
Commoners — Cremation by Pyre
Commoners are cremated on pyres. The body burns with the hair and the Geina.
The ashes are then TBD — scattered? Kept in urns? Buried in family plots? Given
Aicruae Funeral T raditions
6
to a river or the sea? Each choice has very different cultural weight].
The pyre site: TBD — built where? Sacred grove? Temple grounds? Designated
village pyre site? Funeral specifics likely vary by region — coastal communities
may use sea-pyres or boat-pyres given Northern Aicruae's maritime culture;
farming villages may have established communal pyre fields.]
Who lights the pyre: TBD — eldest surviving child? A local priest? A specific
role? This matters for inheritance and family politics.]
Cost: Pyres are not free — fuel is fuel, and the poorest families may struggle to
afford a proper one. There may be temple charity that covers cremation costs for
the destitute, or a "shared pyre" practice where multiple bodies burn together.
INFERRED — confirm or revise.]
Why the Class Split
The Aicruan worldview holds that the soul is what matters most. The hair and the
Geina ritual sends the soul upward in every funeral. The body is what's left over.
For commoners, returning the body to ash and air is the natural conclusion — the
same fire that sent the soul takes the rest. For nobility, the body itself becomes a
political and dynastic object; preserving it as monument keeps the family's
presence in the world.
This split also reinforces class hierarchy in death the same way it does in life. A
noble's tomb is a place. A commoner's pyre is an event. One persists; the other
concludes.
The Procession
INFERRED in part — confirm specifics.]
A funeral procession in Aicruae is a public march. Mourners wearing Iksyres and
Broeps walk together, painted in red, leaving the trail of red footprints. The pace is
slow, deliberate. The chains of the Broeps click as the group moves.
For nobles, the procession may stretch through the capital or a major town, with
the deceased carried on a bier and crowds gathering to watch. The route is
chosen for political and religious meaning.
Aicruae Funeral T raditions
7
For commoners, the procession may be smaller — family and close friends
walking from the home to the village pyre site. But the ritual elements remain the
same: the makeshift Iksyres, the red paint, the bare feet, the trail.
The procession ends at the disposition site — the tomb for nobles, the pyre for
commoners. There the hair and the Geina are burned. The mourners remove their
Iksyres at the end of the rite. The Eye Bind is removed last, by an attendant for
male mourners, signaling the mourner's return to the world of the living.
The Mourning Period
TBD — duration unclear in canon. Some questions to nail down:]
How long is formal mourning? Days? Weeks? A full year for spouses?
Do mourners continue to wear any element of the regalia after the funeral
itself (e.g., a small red mark for a year)?
Are there annual remembrance rites?
How does the mourning period affect work, marriage, public life? Can a noble
in mourning attend court? Can a peasant in mourning be exempted from
labor?
Is there a specific period before the body can be entombed/burned
(preparation rituals, washing, dressing)?
Notable Aicruan Funerals in Canon
Princess Iris Aleka Patton (died 7,218 BR
Killed by Solis at the Battle of Rewqo after being deserted by her knights, captured
alive, escaping, killing 15 men, and being killed by Solis himself. Buried beneath a
temple of Nellebrie at Rewqo.
Prince Orcus Emere Patton (died shortly after Iris)
Buried at the same site as Iris, beneath the same temple. The decision to entomb
them together carries weight given their political opposition during the civil war.
TBD — other major canonical funerals to add: deaths during the civil war House
Orana burned alive — was this a funeral or only an execution?, King Hailour
Layern Patton I, Sevtor of House Orana, Esterica, etc.]
Aicruae Funeral T raditions
8
Open Questions for Future Sessions
The following are inferences I made or details still unconfirmed. Worth nailing
down before this section enters final canon:
Female mourners' equivalent ritual. If men wear the Eye Bind to refuse to
witness, do women have a parallel inward act? Or is the absence itself
meaningful — that women are expected to witness everything, even grief,
while men are permitted to look away?
Specific patterns of the red markings. Are there standard mourning patterns?
Patterns that change based on relationship to the deceased? Patterns specific
to noble houses?
The Broep's "rain of the dead" sound — invented by me or canon? I added
this as descriptive detail. Cut, keep, or revise.
Where ashes go after cremation — scattered, kept, buried, given to water?
The pyre site, who lights it, and what happens for the destitute.
The procession route logic — is it always home-to-disposition-site, or does it
stop at temples, ancestral homes, or politically meaningful locations?
Mourning duration and what wearing/showing of grief continues after the
funeral itself.
Nellebrie's role in funeral rites.RESOLVED Nellebrie is the Goddess of
Disasters. There is no death-specific deity in the Aicruan pantheon. Funerals
are polytheistic — Razar receives the soul, Nellebrie acknowledges the
disaster of loss, and other gods are invoked based on the deceased's life and
the mourners' relationship. Solis burying Iris and Orcus at her temple was
about framing the civil war as the disaster, not about Nellebrie being a death
goddess.
Burial alternatives for the body itself in cremation cases — does anything
physical of the body remain (relic bones, lock of hair kept by family) the way
medieval European Catholic culture preserved relics?
What happens to the Iksyre and Broep after the funeral? Returned to the
temple? Kept in the family? Destroyed? For nobles, are the steel ones
Aicruae Funeral T raditions
9
inherited?
Sourcing Key: Direct canon = drawn from your hub docs and the new funeral
imagery you sent. INFERRED = reasonable extrapolation flagged for your
confirmation. TBD = open question that needs a canonical answer.
Last updated: May 2026  Awaiting clarification on open questions; integration
with Aicruae main page Culture > Funeral Customs section pending.
Aicruae Funeral T raditions

entries.title: Material culture of a pre kingdom warrior age era across six cultural zones
entries.text:
Material culture of a prekingdom/ warrior age era across
six cultural zones
Material culture of a pre-kingdom/ warrior age era
across six cultural zones
The material world of pre-kingdom tribal societies was
far richer, more varied, and more sophisticated than
the "primitive" label suggests. Across every region
that would later become a formal kingdom, Bronze Age
and early Iron Age peoples developed intricate textile
arts, complex legal systems, long-distance trade
networks spanning thousands of kilometers, and ritual
practices that reveal deep cosmological thinking. What
follows is a detailed, historically grounded account of
material culture across six fantasy cultural zones,
organized to provide the specific, textured details
needed to make a mythic tribal era feel real.
The arc across all six zones follows a common pattern:
small kin-based settlements gradually grew through
agricultural surplus and metalworking innovation,
contact with neighbors drove cultural exchange and
conflict, and status differentiation widened until formal
hierarchies crystallized into kingdoms. But the pace,
geography, and character of that transformation varied
enormously.
Material culture of a pre-kingdom/ warrior age era across six cultural zones
1
Equateiy — the Italic peninsula before city-states
Real-world analogs: Terramare culture (c. 1700–1150
BCE), Villanovan culture (c. 900–700 BCE), early
Etruscan/Italic tribal societies
Cloth dyed in bronze-age indigo
Textile evidence from Italy is remarkably rich. The
Verucchio burials (8th century BCE, Adriatic coast
near Rimini) preserved near-complete semicircular
mantles of fine wool in 2/2 twill weave, colored brown
and red, measuring 260 × 70 cm — precursors to the
Roman toga. Their decorative borders were tabletwoven in blue and purple dye. One fragment used
sumak technique of Near Eastern origin, proving longdistance textile trade. A glacier find at Vedretta di Ries
(South Tyrol, 795–499 BCE) yielded preserved underleggings, over-leggings in herringbone twill, and
shoes, with wool stitching dyed using chemically
confirmed indigo pigment. Available dyes included red
and brown (plant-based), blue (indigo), and purple
(possibly murex shellfish, with evidence from Coppa
Nevigata).
Clothing was fastened with fibulae — bronze brooches
that evolved from simple violin-bow shapes in the late
Bronze Age through serpentine, sanguisuga ("leech"),
and dragon types during the Villanovan period. These
weren't just functional; fibula style signaled gender,
marital status, and rank. Elite women wore necklaces
of Baltic amber, striped blue-and-white glass paste
beads, and bone ornaments. Elite men displayed
bronze armor fittings and horse harness gear. GoldMaterial culture of a pre-kingdom/ warrior age era across six cultural zones
2
plated fibulae appear in the richest graves. Evidence
of red face and body paint exists — a custom the
Romans retained for ceremonial statues.
Porridge, millet, and salt from boiled seawater
The staple food was emmer wheat pounded and boiled
into porridge — the ancestor of Roman puls. Barley,
einkorn, legumes (broad beans, lentils, peas), and flax
supplemented the grain diet. Broomcorn and foxtail
millet arrived during the Late Bronze Age through
Carpathian contacts, diversifying agriculture
significantly. Isotopic analysis reveals moderate
animal protein consumption — more vegetables than
meat. Sheep, goats, cattle, and pigs were the four
principal domesticates, with horses especially
prominent in Villanovan culture (evidenced by frequent
bronze horse fittings and artistic representations).
Salt production via briquetage — boiling seawater in
clay vessels — is documented at multiple coastal sites,
including the elite-driven Caprolace lagoon workshop.
Large pottery jars sunk into hut floors stored food,
while sophisticated water management at Terramare
settlements (moats, canals, wells, reservoirs)
supported irrigation agriculture.
From pile-dwellings to hilltop plateaus
Terramare settlements (c. 1650–1150 BCE) were
remarkably planned: trapezoidal fortified villages with
streets in a grid pattern, houses on wooden pile
platforms (even on dry land), protected by earthwork
ramparts and moats fed by running water. Streets ran
1.5–2.5 meters wide; settlements grew from 1–2
Material culture of a pre-kingdom/ warrior age era across six cultural zones
3
hectares to 15–20 hectares supporting 1,500–2,000
people. Over 100 sites are known in Emilia-Romagna
alone.
Villanovan huts (c. 900–700 BCE) are directly
evidenced by hut-urns — cinerary urns shaped like
houses. These reveal circular or oval huts 5–10 meters
in diameter with stone foundations, central hearths,
wattle-and-daub walls, and thatched roofs with
ridgepoles. The great Villanovan settlements occupied
defensible plateaus covering 125–175 hectares
(Cerveteri, Tarquinia, Veii), and the process of
synoikism — villages merging into proto-urban
clusters — transformed these directly into Etruscan
cities.
Crested helmets and antenna swords
Villanovan warrior graves contain the era's most
distinctive equipment: crested bronze helmets with
angular ridges and embossed decoration, bronze
spear and javelin tips, circular parade shields
decorated with rows of raised dots, and the
prestigious antenna sword — named for the curved
terminal pommel. A reconstructed proto-Etruscan
leader from Narce (c. 730 BCE) wore a bronze
"poncho" armor — one-piece front and back plates
joined by straps — plus a crested helmet of riveted
bronze sheets.
The transition from bronze to iron weapons began
during the Villanovan period, with short iron swords
spreading while bronze antenna swords retained their
prestige. Warfare ranged from tribal raiding (mountain
Material culture of a pre-kingdom/ warrior age era across six cultural zones
4
Sabellians "lived by plundering their neighbors'
harvests and carrying off their neighbors' cattle") to
more organized conflict as settlements competed for
resources.
Clans, augury, and the god of boundaries
Early Italic peoples organized in clans (gentes) and
tribes. The Latin tribes formed a federal organization
of roughly 30 communities centered on the sanctuary
of Jupiter at Albanus Mons in the Alban Hills.
Governance evolved from tribal chiefs to kings
(lucumo), recognized by ivory thrones, eagle-topped
scepters, fasces (bundles of rods around a doublebladed axe), and purple robes — all later adopted by
Rome.
Religious authority pervaded governance. Haruspices
analyzed celestial signs and animal entrails to divine
the gods' will; augury directly influenced political
decisions. Dedications to Selvans, god of boundaries,
suggest formalized property dispute mechanisms. The
progression toward formal kingdoms was essentially
theocratic.
Amber, tin, and a Bronze Age trade hub
The site of Frattesina (Po Valley, 12th–9th century BCE)
was a major trade hub, importing raw amber, ivory, and
ostrich eggs while exporting finished goods in glass,
pottery, bone, bronze, iron, and amber. Baltic amber
reached Italy via the Amber Road through Alpine
passes. Tin for bronze production was imported from
Cornwall, Iberia, and Central Europe. Standardized
bronze hoards — broken metal pieces of consistent
Material culture of a pre-kingdom/ warrior age era across six cultural zones
5
weight — may represent Europe's earliest form of
currency.
Biconical urns and the aristocracy of death
Villanovan cremation placed ashes in biconical urns of
coarse impasto pottery, deposited in shaft graves lined
with stones. Some urns were topped with pottery
imitation helmets; others took the form of hut-shaped
urns showing architectural details. During the early
Villanovan phase (960–800 BCE), burial was relatively
egalitarian. By the later phase (800–720 BCE),
dramatic differentiation emerged: elite men received
weapons, armor, and horse fittings; elite women
received weaving tools, amber, glass, and gold
jewelry. The carved wooden Throne of Verucchio —
depicting the entire wool-production cycle —
demonstrates that textile craft was deeply tied to elite
identity.
Gherci — Anatolian highlands blended with Ethiopian
plateau
Real-world analogs: Hatti/pre-Hittite peoples, Kaska
mountain tribes, Phrygians; D'mt kingdom (c. 980–400
BCE), pre-Aksumite Ethiopian highlands
Wool and indigo across two highland worlds
In Bronze Age Anatolia, wool was the dominant textile,
with sheep managed specifically for fiber production.
The earliest evidence of nålbinding (single-needle
knitting) in Anatolia comes from Beycesultan Höyük (c.
1915–1745 BCE), alongside the earliest confirmed
indigo-dyed textile in the region. Common people wore
Material culture of a pre-kingdom/ warrior age era across six cultural zones
6
simple rectangular tunics sewn at the sides; blue
textiles were reserved for royalty and elites per
cuneiform records. The Phrygian soft conical cap
became an iconic headpiece in the early Iron Age.
Romans later called professional embroiderers
phrygiones after Phrygian textile artisans, whose
geometric patterned fabrics were famous.
Jewelry from the Alaca Höyük Royal Tombs (c. 2350–
2150 BCE) was extraordinary: gold and silver fibulae,
diadems, repoussé gold-leaf figures, chalcedony
necklaces, and lapis lazuli imported from Afghanistan.
Common people wore bronze spiral rings and stone
bead necklaces.
On the Ethiopian highland side, early communities
likely wore animal hides and skins, with cotton
domesticated locally but sparsely documented for this
period. The D'mt kingdom's contact with South Arabia
(c. 800–400 BCE) brought textile influences. Ethiopian
megalithic stelae at Tiya feature carved motifs
interpreted as scarification patterns or tattoo designs.
Teff, false banana, and the pig-herding Kaska
Anatolian Bronze Age diet centered on wheat, barley,
lentils, and pulses, with cattle increasingly important.
The Kaska mountain people — crucial for this cultural
zone — specifically raised pigs and wove linen, per
Hittite records. Ethiopian highland agriculture was
distinctive: teff (Eragrostis tef) has been cultivated for
at least 2,000 years; enset (false banana) sustained
dense populations from perhaps 6000–4000 BCE; and
noog (an oil seed) appears at Ona Adi from c. 750 BCE.
Material culture of a pre-kingdom/ warrior age era across six cultural zones
7
Near Eastern crops — wheat, barley, linseed — arrived
by c. 1600 BCE. Evidence for herding at Mezber dates
to c. 1500 BCE, with complex multispecies
management of cattle, sheep, goats, and donkeys.
Mortarless granite and the world's first guerrilla
fighters
Anatolian construction used stone foundations with
mudbrick superstructure — mudbrick that, when
accidentally fired, became "strong as concrete." The
megaron plan dominated: a main rectangular room
with smaller anteroom. At Gordion, Megaron 3
achieved 31 × 18 meters with timber beams spanning
10 meters without internal supports. The Kaska built in
isolated mountain locations designed to leave minimal
trace.
Ethiopian highland architecture reached monumental
scale: the Great Temple of Yeha (c. 700 BCE) used
precisely cut granite blocks weighing several tons,
fitted without mortar, creating an 18-meter-long hall
standing 15 meters high. The Grat Be'al Gebri Palace
(8th century BCE) rose at least 27 meters on five floors
with a 60 × 60 meter footprint.
The Kaska are described as "the first recorded
masters of guerrilla warfare" — concealing
themselves in mountain hideouts, raiding Hittite
territories, capturing cult centers, and plundering
temples. They reportedly fielded 9,000 warriors and
800 chariots. Ethiopian highland tribes used the
plateau's extreme altitude (2,000+ meters) as natural
defense.
Material culture of a pre-kingdom/ warrior age era across six cultural zones
8
Oaths sworn with animal sacrifice
Anatolian pre-Hittite governance was based on
customary authority vested in local chieftains and
religious leaders. The Kaska explicitly lacked
centralized monarchy — they had localized leaders
and town-based identities (e.g., "Kaska of Turmitta").
Ethiopian highland justice systems featured elder
councils (Shemagelle in Amhara; Bayito in Tigray). The
Oromo Gadaa system — now UNESCO Intangible
Heritage — rotated leadership every 8 years through
consensus assemblies held under a sycamore tree.
Blood-price compensation (Gumaa) resolved murder
cases peacefully, with the "dia-paying group"
(relatives within 4–5 generations) liable for payment.
Reconciliation ceremonies included symbolic acts: the
killer wiping the eyes of the victim's relative using
cotton.
Obsidian, ivory, and salt bars as currency
Anatolian obsidian from Cappadocian sources
circulated across the Aegean. The Assyrian karum
trade system at Kanesh/Kültepe (c. 1950–1750 BCE)
imported tin and textiles in exchange for silver and
copper, with authority to fix prices and settle debts.
Ethiopian trade centered on ivory, gold, frankincense,
myrrh, and amole salt bars that served as currency.
The site of Mai Adrasha (c. 1250 BCE) shows largescale metalworking predating D'mt by centuries.
Fetal burials and megalithic stelae
Anatolian burial followed the tradition of intramural
interment — bodies placed within settlement walls,
Material culture of a pre-kingdom/ warrior age era across six cultural zones
9
often in fetal position. The Alaca Höyük tombs placed
bodies with head facing west, face toward south, with
cattle skulls atop several tombs. Phrygian tumuli later
reached monumental scale: the "Midas Mound" at
Gordion (c. 740 BCE) rose over 50 meters high and
300 meters in diameter, containing the oldest standing
wooden building in the world.
Ethiopia holds one of the world's largest
concentrations of megalithic architecture. PreAksumite funerary stelae at Beta Giyorgis (400 BCE–
50 CE) stood 4–5 meters high with vertical notches,
set atop tomb platforms with elaborately decorated
pit-graves 5 meters deep.
Aicruae — Celtic Gaul from Bronze Age through Iron
Age
Real-world analogs: Tumulus/Urnfield cultures,
Hallstatt culture (c. 800–450 BCE), La Tène culture (c.
450–50 BCE), Gallic tribal societies
Striped cloaks, lime-washed hair, and the invention of
trousers
The Hallstatt salt mines preserved the largest
prehistoric textile collection in Europe. HPLC analysis
confirmed systematic use of woad for blue, weld for
yellow, and madder for red, with the earliest confirmed
European textile dyeing dating to the 2nd millennium
BCE at Hallstatt. Diodorus Siculus described Gallic
clothing vividly: "They wear long shirts dyed in various
colors and pants which they call bracae. They also
wear striped cloaks fastened at the neck, decorated
Material culture of a pre-kingdom/ warrior age era across six cultural zones
10
with patterns of tightly packed squares." The bracae
(trousers) were a Celtic invention — the origin of
English "breeches." The sagum cloak was a
rectangular wool piece approximately 168 × 236 cm,
draped over the shoulder and fastened with a fibula.
Torcs — neck-rings of gold, silver, bronze, or iron —
were the supreme Celtic status symbol. The Hochdorf
chieftain (530 BCE) wore a gold-plated torc; the Vix
"princess" (c. 500 BCE) was buried with a massive
gold torc with winged-horse terminals. Warriors limewashed their hair with chalk solutions, sculpting it into
spikes for battle. Woad was used as body paint.
Diodorus describes Gauls with long mustaches
reaching their chests.
The champion's portion and 400 liters of mead
Pork was the most prized Celtic meat — Gaul's cured
hams were exported to Rome as delicacies. The Celtic
feast was a centerpiece of social life. Posidonius
recorded that Celts sat on dried grass at low tables,
"raising up whole limbs in both hands and biting off the
meat." The curadmír (Champion's Portion) — the
choicest cut, typically a hindquarter of pork — was
claimed by the bravest warrior, and disputes over
precedence could lead to single combat. The
Hochdorf bronze cauldron contained approximately
400 liters of mead. Lower classes drank malt beer
(corma); wine was the prestige drink, imported
massively from the Mediterranean after the founding
of Massalia (Marseille) around 600 BCE.
Oppida that required 40 hectares of clear-felled oak
Material culture of a pre-kingdom/ warrior age era across six cultural zones
11
Settlement evolution followed a dramatic arc. Bronze
Age communities lived in open farming villages. By the
Hallstatt period (800–450 BCE), fortified "princely
seats" emerged — the Heuneburg on the upper
Danube featured unique Mediterranean-style
mudbrick construction with bastions. By the Late La
Tène period, massive oppida dominated: Bibracte (200
hectares), Manching (3.8 km²), Heidengraben (16.5
km²). The murus gallicus wall technique — horizontal
timber cross-beams nailed with iron spikes, mortised
to longitudinal beams, with earth fill and stone facing
— required an estimated 700 man-hours per meter.
Bibracte's 5.5 km wall consumed 40–60 hectares of
oak forest.
Sacred spaces centered on the nemeton — sacred
groves for druidic ritual. Viereckschanzen (rectangular
ditched enclosures) numbered an estimated 40,000 in
Bavaria alone, some containing ritual shafts up to 30
meters deep with wooden animal carvings.
Chainmail, headhunting, and the carnyx war trumpet
Celtic armorers are credited with inventing chainmail
(attested by Roman author Varro, 3rd century BCE).
The La Tène iron longsword was primarily a slashing
weapon. Two-wheeled light war chariots replaced
heavier wagons. Headhunting was documented at the
sanctuary of Gournay-sur-Aronde, where a trophypillar was constructed from layered human long bones
around a central pole. Some warriors fought nude
except for torcs and woad, as Polybius described at
Telamon (225 BCE).
Material culture of a pre-kingdom/ warrior age era across six cultural zones
12
The carnyx war trumpet — bronze, ſ -shaped, ~1.8
meters tall, with a bell shaped as a boar's or serpent's
head — produced a terrifying sound. The 2004
Tintignac deposit in Corrèze yielded seven carnyces,
one nearly complete. In 2025, the most complete
carnyx ever discovered was found near Thetford,
Norfolk.
Druids who trained for twenty years
Druids served as judges for all legal disputes —
criminal and civil. Caesar recorded that they trained for
up to 20 years, memorizing a vast oral legal corpus,
and could banish individuals from rituals as the
gravest social punishment. Celtic customary law
(reconstructed through Irish Brehon Law, which
reflects older oral traditions with Indo-European roots)
centered on lóg n-enech ("honor-price") — a
monetary value tied to social rank. Every offense
incurred fines proportional to the victim's status.
Murder required payment to the victim's kin; there was
no capital punishment or imprisonment. Cattle served
as the standard unit of value. Satirizing someone was
legally equivalent to physical assault.
The Vix Krater and tin from Cornwall
Atlantic Bronze Age networks (c. 1350–700 BCE)
united communities from Portugal through Galicia,
Atlantic France, Brittany, and Cornwall. The Nebra sky
disk's tin is isotopically provenanced to Cornwall.
Hallstatt salt mining created extraordinary wealth —
the word "salary" derives from Roman salarium.
Mediterranean wine trade after 600 BCE brought
Material culture of a pre-kingdom/ warrior age era across six cultural zones
13
spectacular imports: the Vix Krater (1.64 meters tall,
208.6 kg, 1,100-liter capacity) and the 2015 Lavau
burial with its Greek/Etruscan bronze cauldron. Celtic
coinage emerged in the late 4th century BCE, initially
imitating Greek gold staters paid to Celtic mercenaries.
Wagon graves, votive waters, and the thin veil
Hallstatt elite were buried under vast tumuli in timberlined chambers with extraordinary goods. The
Hochdorf chieftain (530 BCE) lay on a bronze reclining
couch with 8 wheels, accompanied by a gold-plated
torc, gold dagger, 9 drinking horns, bronze dishes for 9
people, and a Greek cauldron of mead. The Vix
"princess" was laid on a dismantled wagon with a
massive krater and gold torc. Two decapitated statues
at the entrance were possibly ritually "killed."
Celtic afterlife beliefs centered on a parallel
Otherworld — not an underworld but a realm of eternal
youth accessible through water, mist, and burial
mounds. Weapons and treasure were deposited in
lakes, rivers, and bogs as offerings: the La Tène typesite at Lake Neuchâtel yielded thousands of ritually
deposited swords. The four seasonal festivals —
Samhain (November 1), Imbolc (February 1), Beltane
(May 1), and Lughnasadh (August 1) — structured the
year, with Samhain marking the time when the veil
between worlds was thinnest.
Coelum — Atlantic Scotland blended with Norse
Iceland
Real-world analogs: Bronze Age Scotland (c. 2000–
Material culture of a pre-kingdom/ warrior age era across six cultural zones
14
700 BCE), Iron Age brochs, Pictish society, early
Icelandic Landnám settlement (c. 870–930 CE)
Penannular brooches, Pictish tattoos, and vaðmál
currency-cloth
Bronze Age Scottish textiles included wool tabby
weave and bast fibers, with a robust 2:1 twill woollen
cloth found at Oakbank Crannog (Perthshire). Jet
necklaces, gold torcs, amber beads from the Baltic,
and basket-shaped hair ornaments marked status. The
name "Picti" means "Painted People" — likely
referencing tattoos or body paint, though naturalistic
carvings on Pictish stones show warriors and hunters
without obvious marks. Pictish silver chains (over ten
heavy examples survive, some exceeding 0.5 meters)
were worn as choker necklaces, and hipped pins —
bone or copper alloy pins with a swelling at mid-shank
— were a distinctly Pictish form.
In Iceland, vaðmál (homespun wool) woven on upright
warp-weighted looms served as both clothing and
formal currency. The law ounce equaled 6 ells of
homespun cloth two ells wide. Women controlled
weaving and thus currency production. Norse settlers
wore oval "tortoise" brooches, arm-rings of silver or
gold (both jewelry and portable wealth), and fur-lined
cloaks.
Bog butter, dried fish, and barley ale
Scottish Bronze and Iron Age diet centered on six-row
hulled barley with persistent minor oats. Wild foods
included hazelnuts, crab apples, cloudberries, and —
at Oakbank Crannog — opium poppy (interpreted as a
Material culture of a pre-kingdom/ warrior age era across six cultural zones
15
traded exotic). Bog butter — butter preserved in
anaerobic bog conditions — appears widely across
Scotland and Ireland, possibly as both preservation
method and votive offering. Marine resources were
vital in Atlantic Scotland: cod, whale, seal, and
shellfish. Sprouted barley at Culduthel, Inverness may
indicate ale production.
Icelandic diet was dominated by sheep, fish, and dairy.
Dried fish (harðfiskur), reduced to 9% of its original
weight, was eaten with butter at every meal and
functioned as "daily bread." Skyr — a thick cultured
dairy product between yogurt and fresh cheese — was
a recipe brought from Norway that survived only in
Iceland. Meat was preserved by fermenting in sour
whey, smoking, drying, and salting.
Brochs, crannogs, and turf longhouses
Scotland produced some of the most distinctive
architecture in prehistoric Europe. Brochs — drystone
hollow-walled towers up to 13+ meters high — are
unique to Scotland, with 571 candidate sites identified.
Mousa Broch (Shetland) is the tallest surviving
prehistoric building in Britain. Double-walled
construction incorporated internal stairways between
walls. Crannogs — artificial island dwellings built in
lochs — originated in the Neolithic and continued
through the Pictish period. Roundhouses reached 15
meters in diameter (Carnoustie Structure 6), while
souterrains (over 400 underground stone-lined
chambers) served as grain storage.
Icelandic turf longhouses used stone foundations,
Material culture of a pre-kingdom/ warrior age era across six cultural zones
16
wooden frames of birch and driftwood, double-layered
turf walls, and turf-covered gabled roofs. Animal
bones were intentionally buried under foundations as
offerings. The classic skáli (hall) had a central longfire, raised sleeping platforms, and a high-seat flanked
by ceremonial pillars. At Hofstaðir (Mývatn), a grand
chieftain's hall demonstrated the form's monumental
potential.
Scotland's stone circles — Callanish (Isle of Lewis, c.
2900–2600 BCE, stones of Lewisian gneiss up to 4.8
meters tall) and the Ring of Brodgar (Orkney, c. 2600–
2400 BCE, 104-meter diameter, stones from at least 7
different quarries representing different communities)
— were sacred gathering sites spanning millennia.
Kilmartin Glen contains 150 prehistoric sites within 10
kilometers.
Cattle raiding, blood-feuds, and brochs as bastions
Bronze Age Scottish weapons progressed from
daggers through rapiers to leaf-shaped swords. The
Carnoustie Hoard (c. 1120–920 BCE) contained a
complete bronze sword with a hazel-wood scabbard,
showing signs of actual battle use. Pictish carved
stones depict horsemen, foot warriors with spears and
swords, and hunting scenes — the Aberlemno
Churchyard stone likely depicts the Battle of
Nechtansmere (685 CE). Cattle raiding was central to
both Scottish and Norse warrior culture, functioning as
economic warfare and status competition.
Blood-feuds could escalate through generations. In
Iceland's fragmented landscape, warfare favored
Material culture of a pre-kingdom/ warrior age era across six cultural zones
17
ambush and feuding over siege — the lack of forests
meant no castles. Geography dominated tactics:
Scotland's brochs controlled narrow coastal
approaches, while Iceland's open terrain shaped
different conflict patterns.
The world's oldest parliament and the law spoken
aloud
Iceland's legal system was remarkably sophisticated.
39 goðar (chieftain-priests) each held a goðorð — an
office that was not territorial but marketable property,
buyable, sellable, and inheritable. Free men chose
which goði to follow. The Althing (founded c. 930 CE at
Þingvellir) is recognized as the world's oldest
surviving parliament. The Law Speaker recited onethird of the entire law code annually from the Law
Rock, completing the full recitation over three years,
using rhythmic and alliterative patterns as memory
aids.
Critically, courts rendered verdicts but had no
executive power — enforcement fell to the injured
party and their kin. Full outlawry (skóggangur) was the
most severe punishment: permanent banishment,
property confiscated, legal to kill the outlaw.
Holmgang — ritualized single combat to resolve
disputes — was abolished in 1006 CE after abuse by
professional duelists extorting property.
Ship burials and the road to Valhalla
Scottish Bronze Age burials used stone-lined cists
under cairns, with gender differentiation appearing
early: men received archery equipment and daggers,
Material culture of a pre-kingdom/ warrior age era across six cultural zones
18
women received different ornaments. The remarkable
Cladh Hallan mummies (South Uist, 1600–1300 BCE)
were bodies preserved in peat bogs then kept in
houses before eventual burial. Pictish carved stones —
over 350 surviving — used approximately 50 different
symbols (crescent-and-V-rod, double-disc-and-Z-rod,
the enigmatic Pictish Beast) in paired arrangements
that may represent names, lineages, or marriage
alliances.
Norse burials placed the deceased in boats with grave
goods. The Ardnamurchan boat burial (2011) — a rare
mainland Scottish Viking burial — contained sword,
shield, spear, axe, and bronze ring pin. The Norse
conceived of multiple afterlife realms: Valhalla for
warriors chosen by Odin, Fólkvangr for those received
by Freyja, and Hel for the rest. The soul was not
singular — one part might linger in the burial mound,
another join ancestors, another be reborn in a
descendant.
Long northern winters shaped a rich indoor culture:
hnefatafl (a strategy board game found in Viking
burials), saga recitation, weaving, wood carving, and
metalworking filled dark months. The baðstofa
(communal living room) was the center of Icelandic
winter life.
Vikistv — Korean confederacies on a Tibetan highland
Real-world analogs: Mumun pottery period (c. 1500–
300 BCE), Samhan confederacies, Gaya confederacy
(42–532 CE); Zhang Zhung kingdom, pre-imperial
Material culture of a pre-kingdom/ warrior age era across six cultural zones
19
Tibetan plateau
Mandolin-shaped daggers and yak-wool chubas
Korean Bronze Age textiles were primarily hemp and
ramie, with silk introduced later through Chinese
contact. Jade (amazonite) beads are found extensively
in Mumun-period dolmen graves, alongside the
signature crescent-shaped gogok bead — likely
originating from Siberia, representing new life. Bronze
mirrors with geometric patterns were prestige items
used in shamanistic rituals. Chinese records describe
Byeonhan people as practicing tattooing — both men
and women — though tattooing was prohibited under
the Eight Prohibitions of Gojoseon in the north,
creating a fascinating regional cultural tension.
Tibetan highland clothing was fundamentally pastoral:
the chuba (robe) made from yak wool or leather, thick
enough for extreme cold above 4,500 meters. Women
combed hair into many small plaits decorated with
turquoise, copper coins, and shells. Zhang Zhung
kings decorated their crowns with the Garuda (sacred
bird) on both sides.
Wet rice, tsampa, and fermented offerings
Rice arrived abruptly on the Korean Peninsula around
1500 BCE, spreading from southern China. By the
Middle Mumun period (850–550 BCE), both dry-field
and paddy agriculture were intensive — the
Daepyeong site reveals dry-field remains covering
32,500 square meters. Millet was the earliest
cultivated grain. Samhan confederacies held seasonal
sacrificial rites to heaven in May and October with
Material culture of a pre-kingdom/ warrior age era across six cultural zones
20
offerings of food and liquor, singing, dancing, and
feasting.
Tibetan highland diet centered on tsampa — roasted
highland barley flour mixed with yak butter tea —
cultivated on the plateau for at least 4,000 years. Yak
butter tea provided energy and warmth while
protecting lips from cracking in the dry climate.
Nomads above the barley line (~4,500 meters) traded
salt for grain, with annual trading expeditions in late
fall.
Dolmens by the thousands and the Silver Palace of
Garuda
Korea contains the densest concentration of dolmens
in the world — roughly 40% of all known dolmens
globally, an estimated 30,000+ monuments. Three
types exist: northern "table" type with large capstones
on upright stones; "paduk" type on mounds of smaller
stones; and southern type with flat capstones over
buried chambers. The Ungok Dolmen weighs
approximately 300 tons. Mumun pit-houses were
semi-subterranean, evolving from large multigenerational longhouses to smaller nuclear-family
dwellings. By the Middle Mumun, settlements like
Daepyeong sprawled across 243,000+ square meters
with ditch-and-palisade enclosures.
Zhang Zhung's capital Khyunglung ("Silver Palace of
Garuda") sat southwest of Mount Kailash. The military
fortress of Chugtso Dropo on Lake Dangra controlled
central Tibet. Tibetan nomads lived in yak-hair tents
able to withstand high winds and be packed in three
Material culture of a pre-kingdom/ warrior age era across six cultural zones
21
hours, camping in groups of 10–25 families.
Iron empires and horse-armored cavalry
The mandolin-shaped bronze dagger (bipahyeong) is
unique to Korea and Manchuria, distinctly different
from Chinese bronze swords, containing more zinc
and tin. Iron transformed the peninsula:
Byeonhan/Gaya iron was famous throughout East Asia,
attracting traders from Japan and the Chinese
commanderies. Over 350 iron production sites have
been found on the Korean Peninsula. Gaya's most
distinctive innovation was iron plate armor — including
vertical plate body armor and iron horse armor —
found in 5th-century tombs. The Bokcheon-dong
burial ground yielded the largest single-site armor
assemblage.
Tibetan pre-imperial warfare was clan-based, with
horse-based raiding across the plateau. Chinese
sources record that "the men and horses all wear
chain mail armor." Officers carried golden arrows
seven inches long as rank insignia. On campaign,
Tibetan armies carried no grain and lived on plunder.
Sacred sanctuaries where criminals could not be
seized
Korean tribal law centered on the Eight Prohibitions of
Gojoseon, among the earliest codified legal
frameworks in East Asia: murder meant immediate
execution; injury required grain compensation; theft
meant enslavement. The sodo was a holy settlement
controlled by a "Heaven prince" where criminals could
not be apprehended — a sacred sanctuary/refuge.
Material culture of a pre-kingdom/ warrior age era across six cultural zones
22
Political and religious authority were inseparable: the
title "Dangunwanggeom" combined religious (Dangun)
and political (Wanggeom) functions. Bronze bells and
mirrors found in graves confirm that shamans
functioned as tribal chiefs.
Tibetan governance relied on sacred oaths sworn with
animal sacrifice, invoking "the Three Jewels, the sun
and moon, planets and stars" as witnesses. The
Yarlung clan's secret alliance — an oath-based
coalition among neighboring chiefs — became the
foundation of the Tibetan Empire.
Iron as money and salt carried by yak caravan
In Byeonhan/Gaya, iron functioned as a medium of
exchange — smaller iron pieces were "often used as
money." Iron exports to Japan through the Korea Strait
(213 km from Busan to Fukuoka) drove maritime trade
networks. Chinese coins found at Gimhae sites
evidence Han dynasty trade links.
Tibetan nomads gathered salt from plateau lakes and
transported it by yak and sheep caravan to exchange
for grain. Zhang Zhung controlled major transhighland routes acting as intermediary for trade and
knowledge between central Tibet, the Indian
subcontinent, Sogdiana, and Persia.
Feathers for the sky and 32 people buried alive
Korean dolmen burials included bronze daggers,
mirrors, bells, and jade gogok beads — some objects
suggesting the occupant was a shaman-chief.
Byeonhan people buried feathers alongside the dead,
believing they helped souls fly to the sky. Gaya
Material culture of a pre-kingdom/ warrior age era across six cultural zones
23
practiced human sacrifice (sunjang): at Jisan-dong, a
king's tomb had 32 subsidiary chambers for people
buried alive — soldiers, aides, chefs, farmers, artisans,
fishers, even a 7–8-year-old child — intended to serve
the king in the afterlife.
Early Tibetan belief held that the soul resides in the
bones. The first seven kings supposedly ascended to
heaven on a dmu cord rather than dying; when King
Drigum Tsenpo's cord was severed in a duel, formal
earthly burial began — a watershed in Tibetan
funerary culture. Sky burial practices trace preBuddhist roots to Bon body-exposure traditions.
Pireaynea — the tribal Mezzogiorno and indigenous
Sicily
Real-world analogs: Samnites, Lucanians, Bruttii,
Daunians, Messapians; Sicani, Sicels, Elymians;
Apennine culture (c. 1800–1000 BCE), Thapsos and
Pantalica
Tattooed priestesses and the Samnite tunic
The richest clothing evidence comes from
Lucanian/Samnite tomb frescoes at Paestum (4th
century BCE). Samnite tunics were distinctively short
— barely covering the hips — with four regional
variants (Lucanian, Campanian, Apulian, Nolan) in red,
white, blue, black, and mustard. Unlike Greeks who
relied on embroidery, Samnites dyed patterns directly
into fabrics. Women wore scarves and turban-like
hats; men decorated armor with gold and silver inlays.
The Daunian stelae — over 2,000 anthropomorphic
Material culture of a pre-kingdom/ warrior age era across six cultural zones
24
stone monuments from Siponto (7th–6th centuries
BCE) — reveal a critical detail: Daunian tattooing.
Forearms were the most commonly tattooed body
parts, symbolizing sexual maturity, ancestry, tribal
affiliation, and religious beliefs. Unlike Greco-Roman
punitive tattooing, Daunian tattoos were marks of
honor. Women played the chief role in both performing
and wearing them — a practice shared with Illyrian and
Thracian cultures across the Adriatic.
Transhumance, sacred springs, and the Oenotrian
winemakers
Southern Italian Bronze Age diet included barley,
einkorn, emmer wheat, and — critically — early olive
cultivation and possible oil production, documented at
proto-Apennine sites. The "Mediterranean Triad"
(grains, olives, grapes) was establishing itself well
before Greek colonization. The Oenotrians, whose
name means "wine-makers," formed the substrate for
later Lucanian and Bruttian peoples.
Transhumance — seasonal migration of herds
between mountain and lowland pastures along tratturi
(drove roads) — was central to Samnite pastoral
economy. Heracles/Hercules was worshipped as
protector of pastoralism. The ver sacrum (sacred
spring) was a foundational ritual: all products of a year
were sacrificed, including — by tradition — infants
offered to the god Mamers.
Five thousand tombs carved into canyon walls
Southern Italian settlements shifted dramatically
around 1300 BCE, when coastal communities were
Material culture of a pre-kingdom/ warrior age era across six cultural zones
25
suddenly abandoned for inland hilltop positions —
suggesting growing insecurity, possibly linked to Sea
Peoples disruptions. Samnite architecture featured
polygonal wall construction using massive irregular
limestone blocks fitted without mortar. A 2024 LiDAR
survey identified 95 previously unknown hillforts
across 5,900 square miles.
Sicily produced spectacular Bronze Age sites.
Thapsos (c. 1500–1200 BCE) was the first known
"city" in Sicily — a grid-like town with streets up to 4
meters wide, spacious courtyard houses, and a
necropolis of 300 artificial cave tombs. Pantalica
(13th–7th centuries BCE) contained approximately
5,000 rock-cut tombs in five necropoli carved into
canyon walls, with the Anaktoron ("Prince's Palace")
showing Mycenaean architectural influence. The
Castelluccio culture (c. 2200–1500 BCE) produced
tomb entrances closed with limestone slabs carved
with spiral symbolic designs — rare prehistoric
sculpture.
The warriors Rome feared most
Samnite warriors wore Samno-Attic helmets with ear
cutouts, horsehair crests and feather decorations, and
the distinctive three-disk armor (cardiophylax).
Primary weapons were spears and javelins, with
Greek-derived swords as secondary arms. The elite
legio linteata ("linen legion") took oaths never to flee
and carried gold- and silver-inlaid shields. Rome's
adoption of the manipular formation — the military
innovation that built an empire — came directly from
Material culture of a pre-kingdom/ warrior age era across six cultural zones
26
fighting and losing to Samnites in their mountainous
homeland. The scutum (large curved rectangular
shield) was inherited from Italic models.
Lucanian tomb paintings at Paestum heavily feature
mounted warriors, chariot races, and duels — the
"Return of the Warrior" (horseman greeted by
household) is the most common funerary motif,
revealing a society where military prowess was central
to identity.
The meddíss and sanctuaries as neutral ground
Samnite governance operated through a hierarchical
but decentralized system: vici (settlements) grouped
into pagi (cantons) under elected magistrates called
meddíss, grouped into touto (tribal units) under a
supreme meddíss túvtiks. Four touto — Hirpini,
Caudini, Caraceni, and Pentri — comprised the
confederation. The Kombennio was the democratic
assembly responsible for electing officials and making
laws. Confederation-wide action required unanimous
agreement of tribal leaders.
Sanctuaries functioned as neutral meeting grounds
where leaders negotiated and resolved conflicts.
Pietrabbondante — "the cult site of the Safinim" —
fostered ethnic unity across tribal boundaries. The
Tabula Bantina preserves Oscan legal text detailing
judiciary procedures; the Cippus Abellanus records
boundary agreements between communities.
Lipari obsidian — the oldest trade good in the
Mediterranean
The Aeolian island of Lipari was a major obsidian
Material culture of a pre-kingdom/ warrior age era across six cultural zones
27
source found at over 200 archaeological sites across
the Mediterranean — one of the oldest trade goods in
the region. Obsidian was transported as preformed
cores, then reduced at destination sites. With the
spread of metals, obsidian trade collapsed,
devastating the Aeolian economy. Mycenaean pottery
reached Sicily extensively; amber arrived from the
Baltic via Alpine passes; and Sila pitch (bruttia pix)
from Calabria's forests — used for waterproofing ships
and containers — became a major export.
Painted tombs and the warrior's return
The approximately 200 painted Lucanian tombs at
Paestum (4th century BCE) are among the most vivid
windows into southern Italic death culture. Painted in
fresco technique on smoothed travertine, recurring
themes include the warrior's departure for the
underworld, prothesis scenes of the deceased on a
deathbed, boxing contests, and chariot races —
executed in red, yellow, orange, blue, green, black, and
brown pigments. Gender differentiation was stark:
men buried with weapons, women with spindles and
jewelry, though some young women received items
traditionally associated with boys.
At Grotta della Monaca (Calabria), recent 2025 DNA
analysis of Bronze Age cave burials revealed that
interments were organized by sex and kinship — the
dead were sorted by their relationships to the living. At
Toppo d'Aguzzo, a two-tier grave exemplifies
emerging stratification: the upper level held fractured
skeletons without goods; the lower level contained
Material culture of a pre-kingdom/ warrior age era across six cultural zones
28
males with bronze weapons and females with beaded
jewelry.
What drove the transformation from tribes to kingdoms
Across all six cultural zones, the same forces pushed tribal societies toward
formal kingdoms, though the specific catalyst varied by region.
Metallurgical revolution was the most consistent driver. The shift from bronze to
iron democratized access to tools and weapons (iron ore was far more common
than tin), enabling larger armies and more productive agriculture. In Gaya, iron
production directly created the economic surplus that transformed a loose
confederacy into a proto-state. In Italy, control of Tuscan copper and iron mines
gave Villanovan settlements the wealth to urbanize. In Celtic Gaul, Hallstatt salt
mining and control of Mediterranean trade routes created "princely seats" with
enough accumulated wealth to dominate surrounding communities.
Population growth through agricultural surplus consistently preceded political
centralization. The introduction of millet diversified Italian Bronze Age farming;
wet rice transformed Korean subsistence; highland barley sustained Tibetan
plateau communities. Each innovation supported larger, denser populations that
outgrew clan-based governance.
Long-distance trade created wealth disparities that eroded egalitarian tribal
structures. At Frattesina, at Hallstatt, along the Ethiopian Red Sea routes, at Gaya's
iron-export ports — wherever trade concentrated, elite differentiation followed.
Grave goods tell the story clearly: early Villanovan burials were roughly equal;
within two centuries, some graves held gold while others held nothing.
Contact with more complex neighbors catalyzed state formation. Greek colonies in
southern Italy and Sicily introduced coinage, literacy, and monumental
architecture that indigenous peoples adapted. South Arabian merchants at Yeha
brought building techniques and political models. The Assyrian karum system at
Kanesh showed Anatolians how trade could be institutionalized. In every zone, the
pre-kingdom era ended not in isolation but through encounter.
The material culture detailed above reveals that these "tribal" societies were
neither simple nor static. They produced textiles of extraordinary sophistication,
built structures that still stand, developed legal systems of remarkable nuance,
and maintained trade networks spanning continents. The mythic era before
kingdoms was not a void waiting to be filled — it was a world as rich and complex
as what followed it.

entries.text:
A CROWN OF GLORY BOOK
INFO
A CROWN OF GLORY BOOK INFO
Characters from The Book:Minara Gonia The Lost Princess), Nivaeran Veir,
Dahnyliein Catern, Empress Macenja Vandrea), Elleraian Betenadia Patton,Isaeri
Ashonve, Karniode Vesmen, Vasert Prairn, Silaena Chairameron, Professor
Leranoan Gevhilem(Soli), Renedin.
MINARA GONIA
The True Eclipsing Sun / Team Leader, Special Division]
BASIC INFORMATION
fulumu
Full Name: Minara Gonia (birth name unknown - raised under
Siadou Goniaʼs surname; true name would be Minara
Patton as daughter of Emperor Veo Olem Patton)
Book: A Crown of Glory
Nicknames/Aliases: Code Name “Bura” Special Division)
Birth: Dar 27th, 2632 AR | Small village in the Eriata
District, Kingdom of Atriki (south of Elgan) - though actually born in the Imperial
Palace in Bela, then smuggled out
Death: N/A - survives the events of Crown of Glory
Age at Story Start: 17
Book(s) Featured In: A Crown of Glory Book 4
PHYSICAL DESCRIPTION
Ethnicity: Mixed Half Black, Half White)
Height/Build:
Distinguishing Features: Striking fair peach complexion with subtle warmth across
high cheekbones. Large, almond-shaped eyes with vivid emerald green irises
flecked with pale blue - arresting, slightly otherworldly quality. Softly arched, full
brows in
56′ 1/2
A  CROWN OF GLOR Y  BOOK INFO
1
light sandy blonde. Loose, cascading curls of pale honey blonde hair. Heartshaped face - broad at temples and cheekbones, tapering to a gently pointed
chin. Straight, refined nose. Full, well-defined mouth with pronounced Cupidʼs
bow on upper lip; lower lip softly rounded and slightly pouty.
Typical Attire:
How Others Describe Them:
FAMILY & RELATIONSHIPS
Parents: Biological - Emperor Veo Olem Patton (father) & Empress Macenja
Lorafonmenti Patton / Vandrea (mother). Adoptive - Siadou Gonia (raised Minara
as her own daughter; deceased, killed in the Massacre at Aresada)
Siblings: Half-brother - Elleraian Betenadia Patton Crown Prince, first publicly
recognized Eclipsing Sun)
Spouse(s)/Romantic Interests: Nivaeran Veir (love interest →  couple name
“Nivara”). Dahnyliein Catern (arranged fiancé - political match only, never
romantic)
Children: None
Key Relationships: Nivaeran Veir (love interest, confidant - patiently helps her
unlearn hatred of nobles), Dahnyliein Catern (fiancé turned genuine friend initially
hostile, grows into mutual respect), Elleraian Betenadia Patton (half-brother -
doesnʼt learn this until late in the story; she calls him “Ellis Patton” affectionately),
Professor Leranoan/Soli (mentor - she challenges him to practice what he
preaches), Siadou Gonia (adoptive mother her death drives Minaraʼs hatred of
nobles), Empress Macenja/Vandrea (biological mother and primary antagonist -
neither knows their true relationship for most of the story)
BACKGROUND
Childhood: Born in the Imperial Palace as the firstborn daughter of Emperor Veo
Olem Patton. Empress Macenja ordered her execution at birth for being female -
she wanted a male heir of pure royal blood. Siadou Gonia, one of the Empressʼs
personal maids, rescued the infant before the execution could occur and fled to a
remote village in the Eriata District. Minara was raised as an ordinary peasant
child. Siadou never revealed the truth and died before Minara was old enough to
ask meaningful questions. Once joyful and spirited as a child.
A  CROWN OF GLOR Y  BOOK INFO
2
Formative Events: The Massacre at Aresada - imperial enforcers attacked her
village under the pretense of collecting overdue taxes. Minaraʼs beloved mother
Siadou was killed before her eyes. The entire village was slaughtered. This
shattered her innocence and created her deep hatred for nobles and the imperial
system. After the massacre, spent years in a dreary orphanage where she was
locked in a cellar for asking for more bread.
Education/Training: Solisian Academy - entered when the Catern family purchased
her as a bride for their heir Dahnyliein. Gnati division Uncontrolled Magic).
Before the Story Begins: Traumatized orphan with a deep hatred for all nobles.
Fiercely independent, wary, fueled by quiet need for revenge against the
aristocracy. Just before coming of age (and being cast out of the orphanage), the
Catern family selects her as Dahnylieinʼs future bride. She reluctantly agrees,
realizing it may be her only chance to escape poverty.
PERSONALITY
Core Traits: Determined, hot-headed, fiercely independent, wary, compassionate
beneath her walls, morally courageous. Around people who know her: quiet,
understanding, and crazy/energetic.
Greatest Fear: Being alone. Being the cause of everyoneʼs pain / the reason
people get hurt.
Greatest Desire: TBD - evolves from revenge to protecting the people sheʼs come
to love]
Fatal Flaw: Her hatred - blanket rage against all nobles blinds her to allies and
nearly consumes her
Secret They Keep: She doesnʼt know her own secret — her royal identity is hidden
even from herself
What They Want vs What They Need: Wants revenge against the aristocracy that
destroyed her life. Needs to learn that not all nobles are cruel, and that mercy
breaks cycles where violence perpetuates them.
Inner Strength: Integrity, determination, common sense
Kryptonite: PTSD - she has a mild version from witnessing her motherʼs death.
BELIEFS & VALUES
Religious Affiliation:
Political Stance: Begins deeply anti-imperial, anti-noble.
A  CROWN OF GLOR Y  BOOK INFO
3
Evolves as she recognizes complexity within the system.
Moral Code: Protect the vulnerable. Donʼt become the thing you hate.
Life Lesson: “Revenge does not have to beget Revenge.”
Itʼs okay to let things go and forgive.
Disbelief What They Refuse to Accept): You should take everything life gives you.
She is so stuck in her grief for her mother at one point that she believes
everything that must happen has to happen.
What They Would Kill For:
What They Would Die For: Her brother Elleraian, her found
family in the Special Division
True Happiness: Being able to live a comfortable life with her family and friends.
LIKES & DISLIKES
##
Best Thing in Life / Favorite Thing: Her friends and her half-brother Ellis Patton
Elleraian), who help bring back her sense of joy and belonging.
Less Than Favorite Things: Bugs, Homework, and Kiwis.
ABILITIES & SKILLS
##
Magic (if applicable):
Division: Gnati Uncontrolled Magic)
Level: TBD - tremendous raw power]
Specific Abilities: Possesses enormous but unstable magical power. Can
communicate with demons (they understand her and she them - discovered
during the story). With Soliʼs help, capable of guiding corrupted souls into the
great emptiness.
Combat Skills:
Other Talents: Practical survival skills from her peasant upbringing (e.g., baking
bread, resourcefulness with money - stops the group from spending 40 Rern on
bread and makes it herself)
Weaknesses: Gnati magic is as likely to harm her as the target. Overuse risks
aging, madness, and attracting demons. Her hatred and anger can cloud her
judgment.
A  CROWN OF GLOR Y  BOOK INFO
4
ARC & DEVELOPMENT
##
Where They Start: Bitter, traumatized orphan who hates all
nobles and wants revenge. Cold exterior, walls up against everyone.
Key Turning Points: Meeting Nivaeran (first crack in her walls), saving Elleraian
during the demon attack on the Academy (earns recognition), the bread scene
(growth from resentment to generosity), discovering Elleraian is her half-brother,
learning her true identity as the real princess, the Nightmare Realm Trial, the final
confrontation with Vandrea.
Where They End: Chooses mercy over revenge - ensures Vandreaʼs corrupted
soul enters the great emptiness rather than eternal despair. The girl who wanted
nobles to suffer saves the soul of the woman who would have had her executed.
Theme They Embody: Breaking the cycle of violence and revenge through mercy.
“Crown of Glory” - her birthright to the throne she never knew existed.
ROLE IN STORY
Narrative Function: Protagonist. The reincarnation that closes the 10,000-year
cycle of revenge. Through her mercy toward Vandrea, the three sisters Enyokia,
Vandrea, Apharia) finally reunite and can reincarnate together.
Key Scenes: Massacre at Aresada, arrival at Academy, meeting Nivaeran, saving
Elleraian from demons, sleepwalking/lake incident Valoka attack), the bread
scene, discovering she can talk to demons, the Nightmare Realm Trial, learning
her true identity, final battle, choosing to save Vandreaʼs soul.
Relationships That Drive Plot: Nivaeran (humanizes her), Dahnyliein (mirrors her
growth), Elleraian (the brother connection raises stakes), Leranoan/Soli (the
mentor whose own wisdom she throws back at him),
Vandrea (the mother/villain she doesnʼt know sheʼs connected to)
Impact on Other Characters: Transforms Dahnyliein from cold aristocrat to
someone who defends commoners.
Gives Soli a reason to stop watching the world burn. Shows Vandrea mercy when
no one else would.
CHARACTER INSPIRATION
A  CROWN OF GLOR Y  BOOK INFO
5
Real-World/Media Inspirations:
Archetype(s): Hidden royalty, reluctant hero, chosen one (with the subversion that
her “choice” is mercy, not violence)
Voice/Tone When Writing Them:
QUOTES
Memorable Lines: See QUOTE BANK  Book 4 Crown of Glory, Minara Gonia
section 6 quotes filed)
NOTES
Hidden identity: True princess, doesnʼt know it
Mother: Empress Macenja (actually Vandrea in disguise)
Rescue: Siadou Gonia Empressʼs maid) rescued her when Macenja ordered
execution for being female
Escape: Fled to Kingdom of Atriki, Eriata District south of Elgan
Raised as ordinary peasant, Siadou never revealed truth, died before Minara could
ask questions
Empress believes baby died as ordered
Magic: Gnati division (uncontrolled/raw)
Reincarnation: The reincarnation of Soli and Aphariaʼs
daughter (child Vapaz killed during War of Gods II
Special Division: Team Leader, Code Name Bura
Couple name with Nivaeran: “Nivara”
Zodiac sign: Darzi Deceitful, Humorous, Committed)
Birthday: Dar 27th, 2632 AR
Ethnicity: Mixed Half Black, Half White)
Height:
PTSD Mild version from witnessing her motherʼs death
Nickname for Elleraian: “Ellis Patton”
Unresolved Questions: What is Minaraʼs birth name (if different from Minara)? How
does her ability to communicate with demons connect to Gnati magic or her
reincarnation status?
Connections to Track: Siadou Gonia (reincarnation of Enyokia - Minara was raised
by her auntʼs soul without either knowing), Vandrea/Macenja, Elleraian, Soli
Research Needed:

A  CROWN OF GLOR Y  BOOK INFO
6
VANDREA
Grand Empress Macenja Lorafonmenti Patton / The 179th
High Empress of the Solisian Empire / The Reflection of
the Moon Itself]
BASIC INFORMATION
Full Name: Vandrea (true name). Operates as Grand Empress
Macenja Lorafonmenti Patton (stolen identity)
Book: A Crown of Glory (also appears in A Tale of Three Sisters)
Nicknames/Aliases: Empress Macenja, The 179th High Empress
of the Solisian Empire, The Reflection of the Moon Itself
Birth: Date TBD - approximately 10,000+ years before Crown of Glory events] |
Location TBD
Death:  AR | Killed in the final battle. Minara ensures her corrupted soul
enters the great emptiness rather than eternal despair. Reunites with sisters
Enyokia and Apharia there.
Age at Story Start: 10,000+ years old (appears as an adult woman due to
Renedinʼs power)
Book(s) Featured In: A Tale of Three Sisters, A Crown of Glory Book 4
PHYSICAL DESCRIPTION
Ethnicity: White
Height/Build:
Distinguishing Features: Light olive complexion with subtle pink undertones and
smooth, luminous finish. Pale blue-green eyes with piercing, cat-like intensity.
Deep, dark brown (almost black) hair — thick, voluminous, tightly coiled curls
styled with a defined center part. Heart-shaped face with high cheekbones, a
tapered jawline, and slightly pointed chin. Full, dark, sharply arched eyebrows.
Slim, straight nose with refined structure. Full, pouty lips with well-defined Cupidʼs
bow; upper lip slightly thinner than the fuller lower lip. Overall look: dramatic,
sculptural beauty with classical-meets-sophisticated/seductive elegance visually
captivating and memorably intense.
Typical Attire:
How Others Describe Them:
∼2,652
57′ ′′
A  CROWN OF GLOR Y  BOOK INFO
7
FAMILY & RELATIONSHIPS
Parents: TBD
Siblings: Enyokia (older sister - sold into slavery during Solisʼs conquest;
reincarnated as Siadou Gonia), Apharia (younger sister - died during War of Gods
II; was married to Soli; their daughter reincarnated as Minara)
Spouse(s)/Romantic Interests: Emperor Veo Olem Patton (political marriage under
the stolen Macenja identity - not a genuine romantic relationship)
Children: Cevio (first son - died in a rebellion six and a half years before Crown of
Glory events), Minara Gonia (biological daughter with Emperor Veo - ordered her
execution at birth for being female), Elleraian Betenadia Patton (son - publicly
presented as the Emperorʼs heir; biological father is Sir Tonhe)
Key Relationships: Renedin (the Old God who corrupted her soul, preys on her
grief, uses her as his instrument), Enyokia and Apharia (the sisters whose loss
drives everything), Minara (the daughter she tried to kill who ultimately saves her
soul), Soli/Leranoan (her sister Aphariaʼs husband - they fight back to back in the
final battle)
BACKGROUND
Childhood: TBD — pre-Solisʼs conquest]
Formative Events: Emperor Solisʼs war and conquest destroyed her family - older
sister Enyokia sold into slavery, younger sister Apharia killed in the crossfire of the

SERIES PLACEMENT
Crown of Glory is the fourth and final book in the World Without God series. It
takes place approximately 2,632 AR and beyond, during Minaraʼs era. By this
point, Vandrea has positioned herself as Empress Macenja, the barrier between
realms has been weakened for over 2,600 years, and Renedinʼs plans approach
their culmination.

A Tale of a Thousand Songs  BR Solisʼs era)

Crown of Glory brings all threads together. The cycle of revenge that began when
Solis conquered Vikistv and destroyed Vandreaʼs family - over 10,000 years of
hatred - finally ends not with more violence but with mercy. Minara, the
reincarnation of the innocent child Vapaz killed, saves the soul of the woman who
would have had her executed. Vandrea, who chose eternal damnation when she
made her deal with Renedin, is given a path to the great emptiness instead. The
three sisters reunite. The world without its gods finds balance through mortal
heroes carrying echoes of the divine.

PLOT CLARIFICATIONS
Minaraʼs Hidden Identity:
Minara does not know she is the true princess because
A  CROWN OF GLOR Y  BOOK INFO
65
Siadou Gonia was thorough in protecting her secret. When
Empress Macenja Vandrea) ordered the execution of her newborn daughter for
failing to be male, she did not supervise the execution personally. She assumed
her orders would be carried out, as they always had been before.
Siadou Gonia, one of the Empressʼs maids, rescued the infant before the execution
could occur. She fled to a remote village in the Kingdom of Atriki, in the Eriata
District south of the capital Elgan. She never told Minara anything about her
origins, never hinted at royal blood, and raised her as an ordinary peasant child.
Siadou died before Minara was old enough to ask meaningful questions about her
past, taking the secret with her. The Empress believes the baby died as ordered.
She has no reason to search for a princess she is certain was executed at birth.
Vandreaʼs Plans and Motivations:
Vandreaʼs elaborate schemes serve multiple purposes beyond simple
assassination of the Patton bloodline. Direct assassination would be cleaner, but it
would not serve Renedinʼs larger plan. The demon attacks destabilize mortal faith
in divine protection. Each attack that goes unpunished, each prayer that goes
unanswered, weakens the collective belief that sustains the gods of new. This
weakening is necessary for Renedinʼs eventual breaking of the barrier between
realms.
Beyond serving Renedin, Vandrea wants suffering rather than mere death. After
10,000 years of hatred - 10,000 years since Solis and the Solisian Empire
destroyed her family, killed her sisters, and crushed everything she loved - a quick
assassination would be deeply
unsatisfying. She wants the Patton bloodline to watch their empire crumble around
them. She wants them afraid before they die. She wants them to understand loss
the way she has understood it for millennia.
The Macenja Replacement:
Vandrea replaced the real Macenja Lorafonmenti before the imperial marriage.
There was a genuine Macenja, daughter of House Lorafonmenti, who was
betrothed to the Emperor. Vandrea killed her and assumed her identity, using the
shapeshifting and illusion abilities granted by Renedinʼs power. No one detected
the substitution because Vandreaʼs magical abilities are formidable after 10,000
years of practice and Renedinʼs direct enhancement. This deception has held for
decades, allowing Vandrea to position herself at the heart of imperial power.
A  CROWN OF GLOR Y  BOOK INFO
66
The Empressʼs attempts to produce a male heir with other men (knights she had
killed afterward) were part of maintaining her cover. Her firstborn son Cevio was
the son of a famous knight, Sir Joro Noaner; both died during a rebellion  years
before Crown of Glory events. Her second son, Elleraian, is the son of Sir Tonhe -
a grand knight and very distant descendant of Snieoa Patton. Since she failed to
have a son with Emperor Veo, she chose to have children with knights without the
Emperor knowing, having each knight killed for treason before the truth could
emerge. When Elleraian was born with none of the qualities of the royal family, she
convinced the Emperor those traits came from his grandfather on her side.
